extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners and patent practitioners (applicants, attorneys, agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating and preparing affidavits/declarations under 37 CFR 1.130 to disqualify intervening disclosures under AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b) and for invoking common-ownership/joint-research-agreement exceptions under 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(C).

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(1)(B) or 102(b)(2)(B)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the disclosure addressed in the affidavit/declaration is eligible for the inventor-originated disclosure exception of 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(1)(B) or 102(b)(2)(B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 37 CFR 1.130(b) is not available if the intervening disclosure was made more than one year before the effective filing date of the claimed invention (see MPEP § 2152.01). The exception is also not available when the applied disclosure is a U.S. patent or U.S. patent application publication that (1) claims the same or substantially the same invention as the applicant’s claimed invention and (2) the affidavit/declaration contends that an inventor named in that U.S. patent/application derived the claimed invention from the inventor named in the current application (derivation situations). See MPEP § 717.01 subsection II for additional exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of facts, weight and character
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the affidavit/declaration shows sufficient facts, in both weight and character, to establish that the subject matter was publicly disclosed by the inventor/joint inventor or by someone who obtained it from them prior to the intervening disclosure or effective filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the affidavit identifies the subject matter and provides the date of the earlier public disclosure. If the earlier disclosure was a printed publication, a copy must accompany the affidavit (37 CFR 1.130(b)(1)). If not a printed publication, the affidavit must describe the subject matter with sufficient detail and particularity to determine what was disclosed on the earlier date. If the earlier disclosure is the same as the subject matter applied in the rejection, see MPEP § 717.01(b)(2) for analysis. Evidence necessary to show prior disclosure/origin requires case-by-case analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for copies/exhibits with printed publications
rubrics_metrics.description: When the prior inventor-originated disclosure was in a printed publication, the affidavit/declaration must be accompanied by a copy of that printed publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 37 CFR 1.130(b)(1) requires a copy to determine entitlement to disqualify the intervening disclosure under 35 U.S.C. 102(b) and because such information may affect examination of related pending applications (e.g., when the intervening disclosure is a pending application). Exhibits must comply with 37 CFR 1.91 or they may be disposed of or returned. See MPEP § 717.01(d) and § 608.03(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Level of detail for non-printed prior disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: If the earlier inventor-originated disclosure was not in a printed publication, the affidavit/declaration must describe the disclosed subject matter with sufficient detail and particularity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The description must allow the Office to determine what subject matter was publicly disclosed on the earlier date by the inventor, joint inventor, or someone who obtained it from them. Examples include slide presentations, public uses, or other modes of public disclosure; mode need not match intervening disclosure (see separate criterion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal requirements of affidavits and declarations
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the affidavit or declaration satisfies formal statutory and regulatory requirements (oath/declaration content, acknowledgment re false statements, signature formalities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An affidavit is a written statement made under oath before an authorized officer. 37 CFR 1.68 permits a declaration instead of an affidavit; the declaration must include acknowledgement that willful false statements are punishable under 18 U.S.C. 1001 and may jeopardize the application/patent. The declarant must state that statements of personal knowledge are true and that statements on information and belief are believed to be true. See MPEP § 717.01(c) and MPEP §§ 602 et seq. for additional formalities. Exhibits must comply with 37 CFR 1.91.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may sign and who may file
rubrics_metrics.description: Who is permitted to sign the affidavit/declaration and who must file it in the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anyone with knowledge of the facts may sign under 37 CFR 1.130, but the affidavit/declaration must be filed by the applicant or patent owner (or their representative). If an assignee or person with proprietary interest is the applicant under 35 U.S.C. 118, the applicant/representative (not necessarily the inventor) must file the affidavit/declaration. The filing party must have authority to take action in the application; inventors who are not applicants generally lack authority to file. See MPEP § 2155.05.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exhibits compliance (37 CFR 1.91)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exhibits accompanying affidavits/declarations must comply with 37 CFR 1.91 to be entered into the application file.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exhibits not complying with 37 CFR 1.91 may be disposed of or returned to applicant at the Office's discretion. See MPEP § 608.03(a) for exhibit handling. Applicants must include any exhibits they wish to rely upon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness / Seasonable presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: When an affidavit/declaration and other evidence traversing rejections will be considered timely under 37 CFR 1.130.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affidavits/declarations under 37 CFR 1.130 are timely if submitted: (A) prior to a final rejection; (B) before appeal in an application not having a final rejection; (C) after final rejection but before or on the same date of filing an appeal upon showing good and sufficient reasons why it was necessary and not earlier presented (per 37 CFR 1.116(e)); or (D) after prosecution is closed if filed with an RCE (utility/plant applications filed on/after June 8, 1995) or a CPA in a design application. All admitted affidavits/declarations are acknowledged and commented on by the examiner in the next action and noted on the Office Action Summary/Notice of Allowability/Advisory Action as appropriate. Review of refusal to enter as untimely is by petition (not PTAB appeal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Only identical portions are excepted (partial disqualification)
rubrics_metrics.description: An affidavit/declaration can disqualify only that portion of an intervening disclosure that is the same as the inventor-originated prior public disclosure; other portions remain available as prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If inventor disclosed elements A, B, C and an intervening disclosure discloses A, B, C, D, then only element D remains available as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) or (a)(2) as appropriate. Examiners should be aware a 1.130 affidavit may only disqualify a portion of a disclosure applied in a rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mode or manner of disclosure not required to match
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no requirement that the mode (patenting, publication, public use, sale, etc.) or wording of the inventor-originated disclosure match the intervening disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differences in words used or mode of disclosure do not preclude submission of an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.130(b). It is not necessary for the inventor’s disclosure to be verbatim of the intervening disclosure; subject matter identity is the focus. See In re Kao for precedent that subject matter does not change based on wording choices. The affidavit need not show enabling disclosure under 35 U.S.C. 112(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining 'same' subject matter (not 'obvious')
rubrics_metrics.description: The 102(b) exceptions apply only when the subject matter of the intervening disclosure is the same as the inventor-originated prior public disclosure; obviousness is not sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if an intervening disclosure would have been obvious over an inventor-originated disclosure, it is not necessarily the same subject matter; the showing must be sufficient in character and weight to establish that the two disclosures are to the same subject matter. Examiners must evaluate sameness on the facts of each case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Species/genus and genus/species rules
rubrics_metrics.description: How genus/species relationships between prior inventor-originated disclosures and intervening disclosures affect the applicability of the 102(b) exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If inventor disclosed a species and an intervening disclosure later discloses a genus (a more general description), the genus in the intervening disclosure is excepted (not prior art). Conversely, if inventor disclosed a genus and an intervening disclosure discloses a species (more specific), the species in the intervening disclosure is generally available as prior art under 102(a)(1) or (a)(2), unless the genus disclosure would have caused a PHOSITA to at once envision every species (e.g., disclosure of 'halogen' might disclose every halogen element). If the intervening disclosure discloses an alternative species not disclosed earlier by the inventor, that alternative species remains prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to use derivation proceedings instead of 37 CFR 1.130
rubrics_metrics.description: Situations where 37 CFR 1.130 is not available because a U.S. patent or published U.S. application claims the same or substantially the same invention and the affidavit alleges derivation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the rejection is based on a U.S. patent or U.S. patent application publication that claims the same or substantially the same invention, and the affidavit contends that an inventor named in that other document derived the invention from the inventor named in the current application, the proper course is to file a petition for a derivation proceeding under 37 CFR 42.401 et seq. The Office limits availability of 37 CFR 1.130 in these situations to avoid issuance of two patents with patentably indistinct claims to different parties. 37 CFR 1.130 would still be available if the rejection is based on non-patent literature or foreign patents, or a U.S. patent/application that does not claim the same/substantially same invention, or if the affidavit does not allege derivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision authority and review routes
rubrics_metrics.description: Which Office officials decide sufficiency and how refusals/reviews are handled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The primary examiner should review and decide the question of sufficiency of affidavits/declarations under 37 CFR 1.130. Formal sufficiency/propriety questions are reviewed by petition under 37 CFR 1.181 (answered by Technology Center Directors). Review on the merits of a 37 CFR 1.130 affidavit/declaration is by appeal to the Patent Trial and Appeal Board (MPEP § 1201). Review of an examiner’s refusal to enter an affidavit as untimely is by petition and not by PTAB appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art exception under 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(C) (common ownership/JRA)
rubrics_metrics.description: 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(C) provides that disclosures are not prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) if the disclosed subject matter and the claimed invention were owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person not later than the effective filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If properly invoked, the commonly owned or joint research agreement reference is not available as prior art for either anticipation or obviousness rejections. See MPEP § 717.02 for invoking the exception and § 717.02(b) for evaluating applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint research agreement (JRA) conditions under 35 U.S.C. 102(c)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three statutory conditions that must be satisfied for a JRA to establish that disclosed subject matter and claimed invention are deemed owned by the same person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A. Subject matter must have been developed and the claimed invention made by, or on behalf of, one or more parties to a joint research agreement that was in effect on or before the effective filing date (35 U.S.C. 102(c)(1)). B. The claimed invention must have been made as a result of activities undertaken within the scope of the JRA (35 U.S.C. 102(c)(2)). C. The application must disclose, or be amended to disclose, the names of the parties to the JRA (35 U.S.C. 102(c)(3)). The AIA defines JRA as a written contract, grant, or cooperative agreement between two or more persons/entities for experimental, developmental, or research work in the field of the claimed invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of common ownership for invoking 102(b)(2)(C)
rubrics_metrics.description: What 'commonly owned' means for purposes of excepting a disclosure as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(C).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Commonly owned' means the subject matter that would otherwise be prior art and the claimed invention are entirely or wholly owned by, or under an obligation to assign to, the same person(s) or organization(s)/business entity(ies). If the parties own less than 100 percent of the subject matter or claimed invention, common ownership does not exist. A statement such as 'Application X and Patent Z were, not later than the effective filing date of the claimed invention in Application X, commonly owned by Companies A and B' is sufficient to establish common ownership when accurate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establishing common ownership — statement and timing requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: What statement and timing are required to properly invoke the common ownership prior art exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To invoke common ownership, the applicant/patent owner must provide a statement (on or beginning on a separate sheet, not directed to other matters) that the disclosure and the claimed invention were owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person not later than the effective filing date. The statement must be signed per 37 CFR 1.33(b). The requirement is that common ownership existed not later than the effective filing date; a statement of present common ownership alone is insufficient. The question of existence of common ownership is factual for each case; moral or unenforceable obligations do not suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial/common ownership of portions of references
rubrics_metrics.description: How partial common ownership of only portions/embodiments of a reference affects invoking the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no requirement that the entire disclosure in the 102(a)(2) reference be commonly owned. If the subject matter relied upon for the rejection (e.g., first embodiment) was commonly owned, then only that portion needs to be commonly owned to invoke the exception. The examiner may still apply portions of the reference not commonly owned as prior art. Statements can be tailored to refer to specific embodiments or portions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint venture ownership specifics
rubrics_metrics.description: Requirements when applications are owned by a joint venture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For joint venture ownership, both the application and the disclosure to which the exception applies must have been owned by, or subject to an obligation of assignment to, the joint venture not later than the effective filing date. If the joint venture did not own both (e.g., one company owned the disclosure, the joint venture owned the application), the 102(b)(2)(C) exception would not apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licenses and ownership — effect on common ownership
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a license of the claimed invention to another defeats common ownership for purposes of invoking the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A license of the claimed invention where the owner retains basic ownership rights does not defeat common ownership. The focus is on principal ownership rights; as long as principal ownership rights to either the disclosed subject matter or the claimed invention reside in different persons/organizations, common ownership does not exist.
